{{Short description|Object in mathematical sheaf theory}}
{{more citations needed|date=May 2010}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''constant sheaf''' on a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> associated to a [[set (mathematics)|set]] <math>A</math> is a [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf of sets]] on <math>X</math> whose [[stalk (sheaf)|stalks]] are all equal to <math>A</math>. It is denoted by <math>\underline{A}</math> or <math>A_X</math>. The '''constant presheaf''' with value <math>A</math> is the [[presheaf]] that assigns to each [[open set|open subset]] of <math>X</math> the value <math>A</math>, and  all of whose restriction maps are the identity map <math>A\to A</math>. The constant sheaf associated to <math>A</math> is the [[sheafification]] of the constant presheaf associated to <math>A</math>. This sheaf may be identified with the sheaf of locally constant <math>A</math>-valued functions on <math>X</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Does the extension by zero sheaf of the constant sheaf have some nice description? |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4488075/does-the-extension-by-zero-sheaf-of-the-constant-sheaf-have-some-nice-descriptio |access-date=2022-07-08 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>

In certain cases, the set <math>A</math> may be replaced with an [[object (category theory)|object]] <math>A</math> in some [[category (mathematics)|category]] <math>\textbf{C}</math> (e.g. when <math>\textbf{C}</math> is the [[category of abelian groups]], or [[category of commutative rings|commutative rings]]).

Constant sheaves of [[abelian group]]s appear in particular as coefficients in [[sheaf cohomology]].

==Basics==
Let <math>X</math> be a topological space, and <math>A</math> a set. The sections of the constant sheaf <math>\underline{A}</math> over an open set <math>U</math> may be interpreted as the continuous functions <math>U\to A</math>, where <math>A</math> is given the [[discrete topology]]. If <math>U</math> is [[connected space|connected]], then these locally constant functions are constant. If <math>f:X\to\{\text{pt}\}</math> is the unique [[map (mathematics)|map]] to the one-point space and <math>A</math> is considered as a sheaf on <math>\{\text{pt}\}</math>, then the [[inverse image sheaf|inverse image]] <math>f^{-1}A</math> is the constant sheaf <math>\underline{A}</math> on <math>X</math>. The [[sheaf space]] of <math>\underline{A}</math> is the projection map <math>A</math> (where <math>X\times A\to X</math> is given the discrete topology).

==A detailed example==
[[File:Constantpresheaf.png|right|thumb|300px|Constant presheaf on a two-point discrete space]]
[[File:2 point discrete space.png|left|thumb|100px|Two-point discrete topological space]]
Let <math>X</math> be the topological space consisting of two points <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> with the [[discrete topology]]. <math>X</math> has four open sets: <math>\varnothing, \{p\}, \{q\}, \{p,q\}</math>. The five non-trivial inclusions of the open sets of <math>X</math> are shown in the chart.

A presheaf on <math>X</math> chooses a set for each of the four open sets of <math>X</math> and a restriction map for each of the [[inclusion map|inclusions]] (with [[Identity function|identity map]] for <math>U\subset U</math>). The '''constant presheaf''' with value <math>\textbf{Z}</math>, denoted <math>F</math>, is the presheaf where all four sets are <math>\textbf{Z}</math>, the integers, and all restriction maps are the identity. <math>F</math> is a [[functor]] on the diagram of inclusions (a presheaf), because it is constant. It satisfies the gluing axiom, but is not a sheaf because it fails the local identity axiom on the [[empty set]]. This is because the empty set is covered by the empty [[family of sets]], <math>\varnothing  = \bigcup\nolimits_{U\in\{\}} U  </math>, and vacuously, any two sections in <math>F(\varnothing)   </math> are equal when restricted to any set in the empty family <math>\{\}  </math>. The local identity axiom would therefore imply that any two sections in <math>F(\varnothing)   </math> are equal, which is false.

To modify this into a presheaf <math>G</math> that satisfies the local identity axiom, let <math>G(\varnothing)=0</math>, a one-element set, and give <math>G</math> the value <math>\textbf{Z}</math> on all non-empty sets. For each inclusion of open sets, let the restriction be the unique map to 0 if the smaller set is empty, or the identity map otherwise. Note that <math>G(\varnothing)=0</math> is forced by the local identity axiom.
[[File:Constantsheaf intermediate step.png|left|thumb|300px|Intermediate step for the constant sheaf]]

Now <math>G</math> is a separated presheaf (satisfies local identity), but unlike <math>F</math> it fails the gluing axiom. Indeed, <math>\{p,q\}</math> is [[Connected space|disconnected]], covered by non-intersecting open sets <math>\{p\}</math> and <math>\{q\}</math>. Choose distinct sections <math>m\neq n </math> in <math>\mathbf Z  </math> over <math>\{p\}</math> and <math>\{q\}</math> respectively. Because <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> restrict to the same element 0 over <math>\varnothing</math>, the gluing axiom would guarantee the existence of a unique section <math>s</math> on <math>G(\{p,q\})</math> that restricts to <math>m</math> on <math>\{p\}</math> and <math>n</math> on <math>\{q\}</math>; but the restriction maps are the identity, giving <math>m = s = n   </math>, which is false. Intuitively, <math>G(\{p,q\})</math> is too small to carry information about both connected components <math>\{p\}</math> and <math>\{q\}</math>. 

[[File:Constant sheaf with product.png|right|thumb|300px|Constant sheaf on a two-point topological space]]

Modifying further to satisfy the gluing axiom, let  <blockquote><math>H(\{p,q\}) = \mathrm{Fun}(\{p,q\},\mathbf{Z})\cong \Z\times\Z </math>,</blockquote>the <math>\mathbf Z </math>-valued functions on <math>\{p,q\}</math>, and define the restriction maps of <math>H</math> to be natural restriction of functions to <math>\{p\}</math> and <math>\{q\}</math>, with the zero map restricting to <math>\varnothing   </math>. Then <math>H</math> is a sheaf, called the '''constant sheaf''' on <math>X</math> with value <math>\textbf{Z}</math>.  Since all restriction maps are ring homomorphisms, <math>H</math> is a sheaf of commutative rings.
